text: Cornelia Ann Parker CBE RA (born 14 July 1956) is an English visual artist renowned for her sculpture and installation art. Born in Cheshire, England, her early life, marked by a mentally fragile mother and a violent father, significantly influenced her work. Her German mother served as a nurse in the Luftwaffe during the Second World War, and her British grandfather fought in the Battle of the Somme during the First World War. Parker studied at the Gloucestershire College of Art and Design (1974–1975) and Wolverhampton Polytechnic (1975–1978), earning her MFA from Reading University in 1982. She received honorary doctorates from the University of Wolverhampton (2000), the University of Birmingham (2005), the University of Gloucestershire (2008), and the University of Manchester (2017). In 1997, she was shortlisted for the Turner Prize alongside Christine Borland, Angela Bulloch, and Gillian Wearing, who won. She served as Honorary Professor at the University of Manchester from 2015 to 2018 and as Visiting Fellow at Lady Margaret Hall, Oxford from 2016 to 2019, and was appointed Honorary Fellow at Trinity Hall, Cambridge in 2020. Her first solo museum exhibition was at the Institute of Contemporary Art, Boston in 2000; a survey exhibition followed at MCA Sydney in 2019, and a major retrospective opened at Tate Britain in May 2022. Parker has one daughter, Lily, with her former husband Jeff McMillan, and lives and works in London. She is best known for large-scale installations such as Cold Dark Matter: An Exploded View (1991), first shown at the Chisenhale Gallery in Bow, East London, where she had a garden shed blown up by the British Army and suspended its fragments, with a central light casting dramatic shadows on the walls; this inspired an orchestral composition by Joo Yeon Sir. In 1997, she exhibited Mass (Colder Darker Matter), suspending charred remains of a church struck by lightning in Texas; eight years later, she created Anti-Mass (2005) using charcoal from a black congregation church in Kentucky destroyed by arson. Hanging Fire (Suspected Arson) (1999) features charred remains of an actual suspected arson case. The Maybe (1995) at the Serpentine Gallery, London, was a performance piece conceived by Tilda Swinton, who lay apparently asleep in a vitrine; Parker collaborated to create an installation with glass cases containing relics such as Freud's couch pillow, Mrs. Simpson's ice skates, Charles Dickens' quill pen, and Queen Victoria's stocking; a version was later re-performed in Rome (1996) and MoMA, New York (2013). Avoided Object is an ongoing series developed in collaboration with institutions including the Royal Armouries, British Police Forces, Colt Firearms, and Madame Tussauds. Parker has intervened in historical artworks, such as exhibiting the backs of Turner paintings (Room for Margins, 1998) and wrapping Rodin's The Kiss with a mile of string (2003), titled The Distance (A Kiss With String Attached), as part of the 2003 Tate Triennial Days Like These; this piece was later re-staged at the Whitworth Art Gallery, Manchester (2015) and Tate Britain (2022). Subconscious of a Monument (2005) consists of dry soil fragments suspended from the ceiling, taken from beneath the Leaning Tower of Pisa to prevent collapse. These "avoided" objects have been transformed through burning, shooting, squashing, stretching, drawing, exploding, cutting, or being dropped from cliffs; Parker describes them as 'preempted' objects, like Embryo Firearms 1995, or non-objects such as cracks, creases, shadows, dust, or dirt, including The Negative of Whispers (1997), earplugs made from fluff gathered in the Whispering Gallery, St Paul's Cathedral. Another example is Pornographic Drawings (1997), made from ink derived from solvent dissolved from confiscated pornographic video tape by HM Customs and Excise. Parker states: "I resurrect things that have been killed off... My work is all about the potential of materials—even when it looks like they've lost all possibilities." In 2009, for Jupiter Artland, she created Nocturne: A Moon Landing, a firework display containing a lunar meteorite, making the moon "land on Jupiter"; the following year, she made Landscape with Gun and Tree, a nine-metre-tall cast iron and Corten steel shotgun leaning against a tree, inspired by Thomas Gainsborough's Mr and Mrs Andrews, using a facsimile of the gun owned by Robert Wilson, a founder of Jupiter Artland. For the 2011 Folkestone Triennial, she created The Folkestone Mermaid, a life-size, life-cast sculpture of Georgina Baker, a 38-year-old mother of two from Folkestone, celebrating womankind. To mark the 800th anniversary of Magna Carta, she created Magna Carta (An Embroidery) in 2015, a hand-embroidered version of the Wikipedia article on Magna Carta as it appeared on 15 June 2014, completed with embroiderers including members of the Embroiderers Guild, HM prisoners, Peers, MPs, judges, human rights lawyers, a US ambassador and his staff, and public figures such as Edward Snowden, Julian Assange, Jimmy Wales, Jarvis Cocker, and Doreen Lawrence. While the embroidery was on display at the British Library, Parker presented One More Time, a Terrace Wires commission for St Pancras International Station, London, co-presented by HS1 Ltd. and the Royal Academy of Arts. In 2016, she became the first female artist commissioned to create a new work for the Roof Garden of the Met in New York: Transitional Object (PsychoBarn), a scaled-down replica of the house from the 1960 Hitchcock film Psycho, constructed from a salvaged red barn. Parker curated the Found exhibition at The Foundling Museum in 2016, incorporating sixty-eight artists and contributing her own piece, A Little Drop of Gin, a limited-edition photogravure using a 1750s gin glass and droppings of gin, which earned her the Artist of the Year Apollo Award in 2016. She appeared in the BBC Four series What Do Artists Do All Day? (2013), the Brilliant Ideas series (May 2015), "Danger! Cornelia Parker" on BBC One (summer 2016), and Gaga for Dada (autumn 2016), and contributed to the BBC Four production Bricks! (21 September 2016). On 1 May 2017, she was chosen as the official election artist for the UK general election, the first woman to hold that role; she observed the campaign leading to the vote on 8 June and produced two films and 14 photographic works, previewed on BBC Newsnight on 2 February 2018 and made available online via the UK Parliament website prior to an exhibition in Westminster Hall. In 2017, she created a series of blackboard drawings with 5- to 10-year-old children from Torriano Primary School, asked to copy news headlines from UK and US newspapers, noting that at that age children have a barely formed view of the world and will be profoundly affected by political turmoil. In November 2019, she opened her first major retrospective in Australia at the Museum of Contemporary Art, Sydney for the Tenth Sydney International Art Series. In May 2022, she exhibited 100 artworks at Tate Britain in her largest solo exhibition to date, including films such as Chomskian Abstract 2007, Made in Bethlehem 2012, War Machine 2015, American Gothic 2016, Left, Right & Centre 2017, Election Abstract 2018, Thatcher’s Finger 2018, and Flag 2022. Tabish Khan of Culture Whisper praised her work as accessible and playful yet intellectually rigorous. In May 2023, her photograph "Snap" was used as the cover artwork for Peter Gabriel's song "Four Kinds of Horses". In November 2024, her glass rendition of the chandelier from Van Eyck's The Arnolfini Portrait was suspended in the Procuratie Vecchie in St Mark's Square, Venice, as part of Murano Illumina il Mondo, the first time in living memory that artworks were displayed in the colonnade. In 2011, she curated Richard Of York Gave Battle In Vain at the Whitechapel Gallery using works from the Government Art Collection arranged as a colour spectrum. For the 2014 Royal Academy Summer Exhibition, she curated the Black and White Room, featuring well-known artists she believed should become Royal Academicians. In 2016, during her Hogarth Fellowship at the Foundling Museum, she curated a group exhibition titled FOUND, presenting works from over sixty artists responding to the theme of "found". In 2010, she was elected to the Royal Academy of Arts and appointed Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in the 2010 Birthday Honours. She received honorary doctorates in 2000, 2005, 2008, and 2017 from Wolverhampton, Birmingham, Gloucestershire, and Manchester respectively. She won the Artist of the Year Apollo Award in 2016, with shortlisted artists including Carmen Herrera, David Hockney, Ragnar Kjartansson, Jannis Kounellis, and Helen Marten. In politics, prior to the 2015 general election, she endorsed Caroline Lucas of the Green Party, and in 2024 she participated in a plea to end the Gaza genocide. She was appointed Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) in the 2022 Birthday Honours for services to the arts.
